newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Drugs giants, biotechs to hit merger trail.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Drugs giants, biotechs to hit merger trail.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
More big drug makers and biotechnology companies are likely to join the mergers and acquisition dance next year as they seek to improve their products and cut costs.
On Thursday French oil company Elf Aquitaine announced that its Sanofi pharmaceuticals subsidiary would be free to seek a merger with other drugs laboratories.

And on Tuesday Swiss drug titans Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG were given final approval by U.S. anti-trust authorities to merge into Novartis, forming the world's second largest drug company after Britain's Glaxo Wellcome.
Novartis will be capitalised at more than $75 billion.

Last year saw a string of deals, including Upjohn Co of the U.S. merging with Sweden's Pharmacia to form Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc, Hafslund Nycomed AS of Norway joining with Ivax Corp of the U.S. and Glaxo's combination with Wellcome.
Analysts say consolidation among the world's drugs companies is inevitable. Glaxo Wellcome's leading market share is about 4.7 per cent, with Novartis second at 4.4 per cent.
A market share of around 15 per cent, or at least above 12, is considered the ideal target for a viable, high-profit margin operation, although experts do not see this being achieved quickly.
Early in the next century the top 10 might have achieved global market shares of between five and 10 per cent, compared with between two and four per cent now, they say.
This would mean the top 25 to 35 companies slimming down to beteen 10 and 15 over the next decade.
Analysts say this means more mergers, but not only with the big worldwide operations. Smaller biotechnology companies will also be seeking marriage partners to shore up riskier prospects.

"The big corporate guys, and the biotechnology guys are doing things, and it's my belief that both these sectors will continue active in mergers and acquisitions," said Dr Fintan Walton, chief executive of Connect Pharma Ltd.

Walton said big drug companies would continue to seek ways of cutting costs and strengthening their product portfolios. He said companies like Pfizer Inc, Johnson & Johnson, Roche Holding, SmithKline Beecham Plc and American Home Products, would be in the news next year.
AHP announced earlier this week it would buy the 40 percent of Genetics Institute Inc it does not own for about $1 billion.
Small biotechnology firms will also seek liaisons to spread the risk of research and give them more chance of that elusive blockbuster product, according to Walton.
"My feeling is that we will see mergers rather than (hostile) acquisitions, even though these take longer," he said.

Willam Kridel, managing director of mergers and acquisition specialists Ferghana Partners, said he expected more action and felt that companies should be looking to bolster their own specialties, rather than just seeking to boost market share.
"We are finally seeing overcapacity in biotech and you will see mergers, and perhaps hostile takeovers of one biotech of another," he said.
